newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel cuts rates 0.5 point to 14.2 pct.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel cuts rates 0.5 point to 14.2 pct.

text.p: The Bank of Israel said on Monday it was lowering its key lending rate for February by 0.5 percentage point to an annualised 14.2 percent.
The rate is the one charged commercial banks at daily and weekly monetary tenders.

The central bank said it had now cut rates 2.8 points since August from a peak of 17 percent. At the end of December, it lowered rates 0.5 point. Inflation has fallen in the meantime from a 14.6 percent annualised rate in first-half 1996 to less than half that rate in the second, according to Bank Hapoalim estimates.

The Bank of Israel said it decided to cut rates in response to lower inflation and inflationary expectations, which it attributed to the success of its monetary policy. A spokesman also cited the slowing economy. He stressed the importance of the government maintaining budgetary discipline in coming months.
Israeli financial markets had been predicting that the central bank would lower rates between 0.3 and 0.5 point.

"It was (the level) expected, no surprises. They put a lot of pressure on (Bank of Israel Governor Jacob) Frenkel to lower more but he was very cautious. It won't influence shares or the forex market," said Tzvi Hoffman of Meitav Securities and Investments.
He said falling inflation and the exchange rate situation would force Frenkel to continue reducing rates.
The Bank of Israel has had to take into account several conflicting factors in formulating monetary policy.

In favour of easing rates is the lower inflationary trend since the middle of last year, although the December consumer price index was on the high end of expectations. In addition, recent indicators have pointed to a further slowing in the economy, analysts said. The "S" index of economic performance fell one percent over November and December.

Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets, said the latest figures pointed to negative growth in the fourth quarter of last year. He said the economy would grow three percent this year, down from the 3.7 percent he had earlier forecast.
Analysts said the bank also faces pressure to keep lowering rates to prevent the shekel from strengthening too much against the basket of currencies, to which it is officially linked.

However, the central bank must also contend with the budget deficit. Although the official budget aims to keep the deficit to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product, analysts said January spending was probably running ahead of projections.
